Dancing movements that do not result in a displacement of body posture in terms of place is known as ...... Mark Solution There are two major types of movements in dancing. These are: Locomotor movements (traveling movements): These are movements where the body travels through space from one location to another. Locomotor movements primarily use the feet for support however, the body can travel on other parts such as the hands. Non-locomotor movements (movements on-the-spot): These are movements that occur in the body parts or the whole body and do not cause the body to travel to another space. However, non-locomotor movements can be combined with locomotor movements such as a walk and arm swing.

The symbol above can signify: I. Low-pitched notes II. High-pitched notes III. Space notes A, C, E, G IV. Line notes E, G, B, D, F Mark Solution Treble Clef Staff What is a treble clef staff? A treble clef staff is a kind of musical notation used by instruments that have higher pitches. It consists of five lines and four spaces and is indicated by the presence of a treble clef symbol at the beginning of each line. How do I read treble clef notes? Reading treble clef notes requires knowing the pitch that each line and space represents. The lines on the treble clef staff represent the notes E, G, B, D, F from bottom to top. The spaces, also from bottom to top, represent the notes F, A, C, E. What is a treble clef? A treble clef is a symbol that appears at the beginning of lines of sheet music. It tells musicians what the notes of the staff represent and is actually a stylized letter G.

The symbol above can signify: I. Low-pitched notes II. High-pitched notes III. Space notes A, C, E, G IV. Line notes E, G, B, D, F Mark Solution Treble Clef Staff What is a treble clef staff? A treble clef staff is a kind of musical notation used by instruments that have higher pitches. It consists of five lines and four spaces and is indicated by the presence of a treble clef symbol at the beginning of each line. How do I read treble clef notes? Reading treble clef notes requires knowing the pitch that each line and space represents. The lines on the treble clef staff represent the notes E, G, B, D, F from bottom to top. The spaces, also from bottom to top, represent the notes F, A, C, E. What is a treble clef? A treble clef is a symbol that appears at the beginning of lines of sheet music. It tells musicians what the notes of the staff represent and is actually a stylized letter G.

(c) Two issues addressed in King Paluta's Aseda [4 marks] Gratitude and thankfulness to God: the song's title Aseda literally means "thanksgiving"; King Paluta uses the song to thank God for lifting him out of hardship and to remind listeners to be grateful for every small breakthrough. Hard work and perseverance through poverty: he recounts years of struggle, rejection and financial hardship before success came, encouraging young people not to give up on their dreams. The value of family support: he acknowledges his mother and loved ones who stood by him, highlighting the importance of family in an individual's rise. (b) Meaning of the musical terms [10 marks] (i) Presto: a tempo marking meaning very fast; one of the quickest common tempo markings, faster than Allegro. (ii) Allegretto: meaning moderately fast or lightly quick; slightly slower and more relaxed than Allegro. (iii) Andante: meaning walking pace; a moderate, flowing tempo, neither slow nor fast. (iv) Mezzo: meaning medium or moderately; used as a qualifier, for example mezzo-forte (moderately loud) or mezzo-piano (moderately soft). (v) A cappella: meaning in the chapel style; vocal music sung without any instrumental accompaniment. - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section C: Dance Drama

(c) Two ways modern Ghanaian dances preserve and promote culture [6 marks] They keep Ghanaian identity visible to young people: dances like azonto, alkayida and shaku shaku grew from Ghanaian streets, so young dancers who take them up carry Ghanaian rhythm, body language and humour into their daily lives, strengthening their sense of national identity. They carry Ghanaian music and language across the world: these dances are usually performed to Ghanaian songs, often in Twi, Ga or Pidgin; when videos go viral on social media, the songs and language travel with them, exposing foreign audiences to Ghanaian culture. They adapt tradition into a modern form: many of the moves borrow from traditional dances (footwork from kpanlogo, waist movements from adowa), so performing them keeps traditional patterns alive in a shape that feels modern. They become a tool for tourism and cultural events: dance groups use them at festivals, Independence Day parades and shows for visiting tourists, turning culture into a positive economic activity. They teach teamwork and community spirit: most modern dances are group dances, so learning and performing them together builds the kind of community feeling that traditional Ghanaian dance has always encouraged. - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section C: Dance Drama

(c) Elements of contemporary dance, with examples [6 marks] (i) Body: The dancer's own body is the main instrument; every part, from fingers to feet, is used to shape movement. In contemporary dance the whole body is available, so a performer might isolate just the shoulder in one moment and involve the entire body in a falling roll in the next. Example: a dancer curls into a tight ball to express grief, then slowly unfolds, using the torso and limbs in sequence, to show recovery. (ii) Space: How the dancer uses the area around them. This covers levels (high, medium, low), directions (forward, backward, diagonal), pathways (straight, curved, zig-zag) and personal space (how close the dancer is to others). Example: a solo dancer moves from an upstage corner along a curving pathway to a low level centre stage, shrinking the space to pull the audience's focus inwards. - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m (iii) Energy: The quality or force behind the movement: smooth versus sharp, strong versus gentle, sustained versus sudden. Changing the energy changes the feeling of the dance even when the steps are the same. Example: the same arm gesture done with soft, sustained energy feels peaceful, but done with sharp, percussive energy feels angry or urgent. (b) Three benefits of displaying works for appreciation [9 marks] Builds self-confidence: public appreciation validates the learner's effort, makes them feel recognised, and reduces performance-related anxiety, which encourages them to keep creating. Fosters creativity: seeing each other's work inspires fresh ideas, encourages experimentation, and allows learners to build on each other's concepts. - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Motivates learners: when their work is seen and admired, learners feel a sense of accomplishment, become more enthusiastic about the subject, and take more initiative in future projects. Improves communication skills: describing one's own work and giving feedback on peers' work teaches learners to articulate ideas clearly and give constructive criticism. Promotes critical thinking: appreciating art trains the eye to analyse composition, technique and meaning, and encourages curiosity-driven questions. Preserves and shares culture: appreciation sessions often surface Ghanaian themes, symbols and values, helping to pass them on. - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m

(c) Two issues addressed in King Paluta's Aseda [4 marks] Gratitude and thankfulness to God: the song's title Aseda literally means "thanksgiving"; King Paluta uses the song to thank God for lifting him out of hardship and to remind listeners to be grateful for every small breakthrough. Hard work and perseverance through poverty: he recounts years of struggle, rejection and financial hardship before success came, encouraging young people not to give up on their dreams. The value of family support: he acknowledges his mother and loved ones who stood by him, highlighting the importance of family in an individual's rise. Humility despite success: he warns that wealth and fame should not change a person's character, a common message in Ghanaian moral teaching. Faith and trust in God: the song frames success as God's doing and calls on listeners to put their trust in God rather than in people alone. - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m

(b) Meaning of the musical terms [10 marks] (i) Presto: a tempo marking meaning very fast; one of the quickest common tempo markings, faster than Allegro. (ii) Allegretto: meaning moderately fast or lightly quick; slightly slower and more relaxed than Allegro. (iii) Andante: meaning walking pace; a moderate, flowing tempo, neither slow nor fast. (iv) Mezzo: meaning medium or moderately; used as a qualifier, for example mezzo-forte (moderately loud) or mezzo-piano (moderately soft). (v) A cappella: meaning in the chapel style; vocal music sung without any instrumental accompaniment. - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section C: Dance Drama

(c) Two ways modern Ghanaian dances preserve and promote culture [6 marks] They keep Ghanaian identity visible to young people: dances like azonto, alkayida and shaku shaku grew from Ghanaian streets, so young dancers who take them up carry Ghanaian rhythm, body language and humour into their daily lives, strengthening their sense of national identity. They carry Ghanaian music and language across the world: these dances are usually performed to Ghanaian songs, often in Twi, Ga or Pidgin; when videos go viral on social media, the songs and language travel with them, exposing foreign audiences to Ghanaian culture. They adapt tradition into a modern form: many of the moves borrow from traditional dances (footwork from kpanlogo, waist movements from adowa), so performing them keeps traditional patterns alive in a shape that feels modern. They become a tool for tourism and cultural events: dance groups use them at festivals, Independence Day parades and shows for visiting tourists, turning culture into a positive economic activity. They teach teamwork and community spirit: most modern dances are group dances, so learning and performing them together builds the kind of community feeling that traditional Ghanaian dance has always encouraged. - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Section C: Dance Drama

(c) Elements of contemporary dance, with examples [6 marks] (i) Body: The dancer's own body is the main instrument; every part, from fingers to feet, is used to shape movement. In contemporary dance the whole body is available, so a performer might isolate just the shoulder in one moment and involve the entire body in a falling roll in the next. Example: a dancer curls into a tight ball to express grief, then slowly unfolds, using the torso and limbs in sequence, to show recovery. (ii) Space: How the dancer uses the area around them. This covers levels (high, medium, low), directions (forward, backward, diagonal), pathways (straight, curved, zig-zag) and personal space (how close the dancer is to others). Example: a solo dancer moves from an upstage corner along a curving pathway to a low level centre stage, shrinking the space to pull the audience's focus inwards. - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m (iii) Energy: The quality or force behind the movement: smooth versus sharp, strong versus gentle, sustained versus sudden. Changing the energy changes the feeling of the dance even when the steps are the same. Example: the same arm gesture done with soft, sustained energy feels peaceful, but done with sharp, percussive energy feels angry or urgent. Notation on the treble staff, classifying instruments, reading a time signature, and explaining binary form. 4(a) Notate ECG, BAD and AGF on the treble staff using minims [6 marks] A minim (half note) is written as a hollow note head with a stem. On the treble staff, the lines from bottom to top are E G B D F and the spaces from bottom to top are F A C E. Place each letter of the triads on its matching line or space and draw a minim on it, repeating the treble clef at the start of each staff. 4(b) Classify the instruments [5 marks] Chordophone: Seperewa. Idiophone: Mbira. Membranophone: Donno. Aerophone: Atenteben and Mmensuon. 4(c) Time signature of the song [2 marks] Four quavers equal two crotchet beats; one minim equals two crotchet beats; two crotchets equal two crotchet beats. Each bar therefore contains two crotchet beats, so the time signature is 2/4 (simple duple). 4(d) Why Yen ara asaase ni is in binary form [2 marks] Binary form means the piece is built from two contrasting sections, often called A and B. Notating semibreves on the treble and bass staves, classifying Western instruments, and interpreting King Paluta's Aseda. 4(a) Notate F, C (treble) and C (bass) using semibreves [6 marks] A semibreve (whole note) is written as an open (hollow) note head with no stem. Treble staff: the five lines from bottom to top spell E G B D F (mnemonic: "Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit") and the four spaces spell F A C E. (i) F on a line in the treble clef is written on the very top line of the staff. (ii) C on a space in the treble clef is written in the third space from the bottom (the C of F-A-C-E). Bass staff: the five lines from bottom to top spell G B D F A ("Good Boys Deserve Fruit Always") and the four spaces spell A C E G ("All Cows Eat Grass"). (iii) C on a space in the bass clef is written in the second space from the bottom (the C of A-C-E- G). Begin each staff with the correct clef sign before drawing the semibreve on the required line or space. 2 marks per correctly placed note. 4(b) Classify the Western instruments [5 marks] Quick check: woodwinds produce sound by a vibrating reed or an edge of air (clarinet); brass by the player's buzzing lips into a metal mouthpiece (trombone); percussion by being struck (cymbals); strings by bowing or plucking taut strings (cello); electronic by generating or amplifying sound electrically (keyboard/synthesiser). WOODWINDS BRASS PERCUSSION STRINGS ELECTRONIC Clarinet Trombone Cymbals Cello Keyboard 4(c) Two issues addressed in King Paluta's Aseda [4 marks] Gratitude and thankfulness to God: the song's title Aseda literally means "thanksgiving"; King Paluta uses the song to thank God for lifting him out of hardship and to remind listeners to be grateful for every small breakthrough. Hard work and perseverance through poverty: he recounts years of struggle, rejection and financial hardship before success came, encouraging young people not to give up on their dreams. The value of family support: he acknowledges his mother and loved ones who stood by him, highlighting the importance of family in an individual's rise. Humility despite success: he warns that wealth and fame should not change a person's character, a common message in Ghanaian moral teaching. Faith and trust in God: the song frames success as God's doing and calls on listeners to put their trust in God rather than in people alone. - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m

Maame Dokono's contributions, performance-space anatomy, and modern Ghanaian dances as cultural promoters. 6(a) Three contributions of Grace Omaboe (Maame Dokono) [3 marks] Promoted Ghanaian storytelling on television: she hosted and starred in By the Fireside, a long- running children's TV programme that retold Ananse and other folk stories in Akan, keeping oral tradition alive for new generations. Built a celebrated acting career: she acted in numerous Ghanaian films and stage plays, becoming one of the most recognised actresses of her generation and inspiring many younger performers. Mentored and trained younger actors: through her productions and workshops she helped groom new talent in the Ghanaian creative-arts industry. Produced cultural content in local languages: her work mostly used Akan, which helped preserve and promote the use of Ghanaian languages in the media. Engaged in public and charity work: she used her public profile for charitable causes and community engagement, serving as a role model for women in the arts. Served in public office: she took on political and public-service roles that extended her cultural advocacy beyond the screen. 6(b)(i) Three parts of the performance space [3 marks] Stage Backstage Wings Auditorium (house) Orchestra pit Apron (forestage) Dressing rooms Green room Lighting booth / Sound booth (control room) 6(b)(ii) One function of each part named in (i) [3 marks] Stage: the main acting area where all performances take place in full view of the audience. Backstage: the area behind the stage used for scenery storage, set changes and out-of-sight movement between entrances. Wings: the narrow areas at each side of the stage where performers wait, hidden from the audience, before making an entrance. - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m Auditorium: the space where the audience sits to watch the performance. Orchestra pit: a lowered area between the stage and audience that houses the musicians accompanying the performance. Apron: the part of the stage that projects towards the audience beyond the main curtain; used for close, direct address. Dressing rooms: where performers change into costume and put on make-up before and during the show. Green room: a lounge where performers relax and wait when they are not on stage. Lighting / sound booth: the control room from which technicians operate the lighting and sound cues. 6(c) Two ways modern Ghanaian dances preserve and promote culture [6 marks] They keep Ghanaian identity visible to young people: dances like azonto, alkayida and shaku shaku grew from Ghanaian streets, so young dancers who take them up carry Ghanaian rhythm, body language and humour into their daily lives, strengthening their sense of national identity. They carry Ghanaian music and language across the world: these dances are usually performed to Ghanaian songs, often in Twi, Ga or Pidgin; when videos go viral on social media, the songs and language travel with them, exposing foreign audiences to Ghanaian culture. They adapt tradition into a modern form: many of the moves borrow from traditional dances (footwork from kpanlogo, waist movements from adowa), so performing them keeps traditional patterns alive in a shape that feels modern. They become a tool for tourism and cultural events: dance groups use them at festivals, Independence Day parades and shows for visiting tourists, turning culture into a positive economic activity. Defining dance-drama, using body parts in performance, and the elements of contemporary dance. 7(a) Explain dance-drama [3 marks] Dance-drama is a form of performance that tells a complete story using dance movements together with the elements of drama: characters, a plot, costumes, music and sometimes dialogue or mime. The dancers act out the events of the story through choreographed movement; meaning is carried by the body rather than mainly by spoken words. It combines the storytelling power of drama with the emotional and rhythmic power of dance, so the audience both follows a story and enjoys the movement. 7(b) How actors and dancers use body parts in performance [6 marks] Feet: establish rhythm and energy. Stamping feet show anger or assertiveness; soft gliding steps show calmness; running shows urgency. Arms: extend the body into space and shape emotion. Raised arms show joy or victory; wide open arms welcome; crossed arms show refusal or protection. Hands: carry detailed meaning. Pointing directs attention; clenched fists show anger or determination; open palms show honesty or pleading; waving greets or dismisses. Legs: create shape and power. Bent knees ground the dancer in traditional Ghanaian style; leaps show excitement; kneeling shows submission or prayer. Head: adds focus and attitude. Nodding shows agreement; shaking shows refusal; a tilted head shows curiosity; a lowered head shows sorrow or respect. Neck: amplifies the head's meaning. A stretched neck shows pride or alertness; a relaxed neck shows calm; a turned neck directs gaze and intention. Torso: is the emotional centre of the body. A lifted chest shows confidence; a collapsed chest shows defeat; a twisted torso shows tension or conflict; hip sways carry the rhythm in many African dances. 7(c) Elements of contemporary dance, with examples [6 marks] (i) Body: The dancer's own body is the main instrument; every part, from fingers to feet, is used to shape movement. In contemporary dance the whole body is available, so a performer might isolate just the shoulder in one moment and involve the entire body in a falling roll in the next. Example: a dancer curls into a tight ball to express grief, then slowly unfolds, using the torso and limbs in sequence, to show recovery. (ii) Space: How the dancer uses the area around them. This covers levels (high, medium, low), directions (forward, backward, diagonal), pathways (straight, curved, zig-zag) and personal space (how close the dancer is to others). Example: a solo dancer moves from an upstage corner along a curving pathway to a low level centre stage, shrinking the space to pull the audience's focus inwards. - - - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m (iii) Energy: The quality or force behind the movement: smooth versus sharp, strong versus gentle, sustained versus sudden. Changing the energy changes the feeling of the dance even when the steps are the same. Example: the same arm gesture done with soft, sustained energy feels peaceful, but done with sharp, percussive energy feels angry or urgent. Notating semibreves on the treble and bass staves, classifying Western instruments, and interpreting King Paluta's Aseda. 4(a) Notate F, C (treble) and C (bass) using semibreves [6 marks] A semibreve (whole note) is written as an open (hollow) note head with no stem. Treble staff: the five lines from bottom to top spell E G B D F (mnemonic: "Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit") and the four spaces spell F A C E. (i) F on a line in the treble clef is written on the very top line of the staff. (ii) C on a space in the treble clef is written in the third space from the bottom (the C of F-A-C-E). Bass staff: the five lines from bottom to top spell G B D F A ("Good Boys Deserve Fruit Always") and the four spaces spell A C E G ("All Cows Eat Grass"). (iii) C on a space in the bass clef is written in the second space from the bottom (the C of A-C-E- G). Begin each staff with the correct clef sign before drawing the semibreve on the required line or space. 2 marks per correctly placed note. 4(b) Classify the Western instruments [5 marks] Quick check: woodwinds produce sound by a vibrating reed or an edge of air (clarinet); brass by the player's buzzing lips into a metal mouthpiece (trombone); percussion by being struck (cymbals); strings by bowing or plucking taut strings (cello); electronic by generating or amplifying sound electrically (keyboard/synthesiser). WOODWINDS BRASS PERCUSSION STRINGS ELECTRONIC Clarinet Trombone Cymbals Cello Keyboard 4(c) Two issues addressed in King Paluta's Aseda [4 marks] Gratitude and thankfulness to God: the song's title Aseda literally means "thanksgiving"; King Paluta uses the song to thank God for lifting him out of hardship and to remind listeners to be grateful for every small breakthrough. Hard work and perseverance through poverty: he recounts years of struggle, rejection and financial hardship before success came, encouraging young people not to give up on their dreams. The value of family support: he acknowledges his mother and loved ones who stood by him, highlighting the importance of family in an individual's rise. Humility despite success: he warns that wealth and fame should not change a person's character, a common message in Ghanaian moral teaching. Faith and trust in God: the song frames success as God's doing and calls on listeners to put their trust in God rather than in people alone. - - - - - - - - D O W N L O A D E D F R O M SRONU p a p e r s . s r o n u . c o m

Features of art music, notes in a 3/4 bar, conducting pattern and triads. 4(a) State and explain two features of art music [4 marks] It is composed and written down (notated) by a known composer using staff notation, so it can be performed exactly as written. It is performed from a score, usually by trained musicians who follow the composer's instructions on pitch, rhythm and dynamics. It uses Western harmony, form and instruments such as the choir, organ or orchestra. It is usually performed in formal concert settings (for example by choirs and orchestras), for example anthems, hymns and cantatas. 4(b)(i) A different set of notes that fit a 3/4 bar [3 marks] The time signature is 3/4, so each bar must add up to three crotchet beats. Any correct combination totalling three crotchet beats is accepted, for example: a dotted minim (3 beats); a minim + a crotchet (2 + 1); a crotchet + four quavers (1 + 2) ... continue to total 3; six quavers (½ × 6 = 3). The set drawn must be different from the one given in the question. 4(b)(ii) Suitable conducting pattern for 3/4 [2 marks] Use the three-beat (triangular) conducting pattern. The hand moves down on beat 1, out to the right on beat 2, and up back to the start on beat 3 (down – out – up), forming a triangle. 4(c)(i) Triad with C as root, treble clef [3 marks] A triad is the root, the third above it and the fifth above the root, played together. Drama terms, and the role of traditional drama in national identity. 7(a) Describe the drama terms [6 marks] Mood and atmosphere: the feeling or emotional tone of a scene (such as joyful, tense or sad) and the overall feeling the audience senses; it is built up through lighting, sound, set and acting. Motivation: the reason or inner drive behind a character's actions; what the character wants and why they behave the way they do. Setting: the time and place in which the action of the play happens (the location and the period). 7(b) Three roles of traditional Ghanaian drama in promoting national identity [9 marks] It preserves and showcases cultural values, customs and language, keeping Ghanaian heritage alive. It teaches history and shared heritage, uniting people around common stories and experiences. It promotes patriotism and pride in being Ghanaian and a sense of belonging. It reflects the Ghanaian way of life through local symbols, costumes, music and dance that mark Ghana out as unique. - - - Each term is worth 2 marks: describe all three (2 + 2 + 2 = 6). Note
